title: Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price
gist: With nearly two-thirds of U.S. federal revenue coming from labor taxes, RAND's Carter Price argues AI job displacement threatens the Treasury and that the tax code (payroll tax, accelerated depreciation) currently subsidizes automation. He proposes replacing the employer payroll tax with a flat business-revenue tax plus a progressive tax on profit per worker, funded by eliminating niche carve-outs and achievable with only an act of Congress.

themes.theme: Federal revenue exposure to AI labor displacement

insights.claim: Nearly two-thirds of all U.S. federal revenue comes from taxes levied on human labor, so large-scale AI job displacement would directly erode the Treasury's revenue base.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: AI-driven layoffs are a fiscal risk: watch deficit projections, Treasury issuance and pressure for new tax bases if labor share falls.
insights.quote: Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue comes from taxes levied on human labor
insights.locator: Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue

insights.claim: Lost labor-tax revenue from AI displacement will not be easy to replace, creating a structural case for rebalancing the U.S. tax code away from dependence on labor income.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Raises odds that future tax reform shifts burden toward corporate profits/revenue rather than wages.
insights.quote: That revenue will not be easy to make up if AI starts to put large numbers of people out of work.
insights.locator: Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue

insights.claim: The employer payroll tax raises the cost of every additional worker, making the current U.S. tax code a structural disincentive to hiring and retaining humans.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Labor-intensive business models carry a tax penalty relative to capital-intensive ones; policy change here would alter automation ROI.
insights.locator: The employer payroll tax is one obvious

insights.claim: Accelerated depreciation lets companies write off big assets such as robotic systems before they wear out, which RAND's Carter Price characterizes as a direct subsidy for displacing human workers.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Automation/robotics capex demand is partly tax-driven; any rollback of accelerated depreciation would hit robotics and AI-infrastructure ROI.
insights.quote: that tax write-off a direct subsidy for displacing human workers
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the tax code allows companies

insights.claim: RAND built a tool that parses all 7,000 pages of the U.S. tax code to identify every provision and its implications, enabling systematic analysis of pro- and anti-employment provisions.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
entities: RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative
insights.so_what: Signals think-tank capacity to produce granular, scoreable reform packages that can move quickly into legislative debate.

insights.claim: RAND proposes a progressive corporate tax on profit per worker, layered on top of the existing corporate income tax, so firms that shed workers while holding profit constant move into higher brackets.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: If adopted, highly automated, low-headcount, high-margin firms (e.g., AI-native companies) would face higher effective tax rates; labor-heavy firms relatively advantaged.
insights.quote: The government would tax high corporate profits per worker in addition to taxing their income overall.
insights.locator: Our idea is somewhat similar, but

insights.claim: Illustration: a company earning $1 million profit with 100 employees has $10,000 profit per worker; cutting to 10 workers via AI lifts it to $100,000 per worker and a higher tax bracket, raising its tax on the same $1 million profit.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Useful screen: profit per employee becomes a tax-exposure metric for mega-cap tech and automation-heavy firms under such a regime.

insights.claim: The profit-per-worker tax is designed not to block automation where AI is sufficiently more efficient; it only removes the tax code's tilt toward replacing workers.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Proposal is framed as incentive-neutralizing rather than anti-AI, improving its political viability relative to outright robot taxes.
insights.quote: AI might still be so much more efficient that it still makes sense for some companies to replace those workers.
insights.locator: AI might still be so much more

insights.claim: RAND's reform package would eliminate the employer payroll tax and replace it with a flat tax on business revenue plus the per-worker tax on high profits, funded partly by eliminating niche tax breaks.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Shift from wage-based to revenue/profit-based business taxation would favor labor-intensive sectors and penalize low-headcount, high-revenue firms.
insights.quote: eliminate the employer payroll tax and replace it with two business taxes
insights.locator: The federal government could then eliminate

insights.claim: The tax code contains many redundant niche provisions, e.g., three separate clean-energy vehicle tax provisions that do essentially the same thing, and breaks benefiting investments in distilled spirits, which RAND would eliminate to raise revenue.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Beneficiaries of niche carve-outs (clean-energy vehicles, distilled spirits) face tail risk if AI-era tax reform seeks pay-fors.
insights.quote: There are three different clean-energy vehicle tax provisions, for example, and they all do pretty much the same thing.
insights.locator: We found a lot of special

insights.claim: Price argues companies in aggregate would be no worse off because lost payroll tax revenue is offset by removing special carve-outs.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Revenue-neutral framing matters for scoring; distributional winners/losers across firms remain large even if aggregate is neutral.
insights.quote: Companies would be no worse off.
insights.locator: Companies would be no worse off.

insights.claim: The profit-per-worker reform needs only an act of Congress to amend the Internal Revenue Code, a lower barrier than a value-added tax (new collection infrastructure) or a federal wealth tax (constitutional amendment plus new infrastructure).
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Among AI-era revenue ideas, IRC tweaks are the most legislatively plausible; weight them above VAT or wealth-tax scenarios.
insights.quote: a federal wealth tax, which could generate revenue from huge concentrations of wealth, would require a constitutional amendment
insights.locator: It takes an act of Congress

insights.claim: Simplifying the tax code would return millions of hours people spend on tax forms and improve economic efficiency.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Simplification could weigh on tax-prep/compliance businesses over time.

insights.claim: AI models have advanced in mathematics and can generate code that would take humans hours or days, but Price believes human mathematicians still add value AI cannot fully replace, though not necessarily forever.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Even domain experts concede eventual substitution risk in high-skill knowledge work, reinforcing the displacement scenario underlying tax reform.
insights.quote: I'm not sure that will be true forever.
